summary: How sound is digitised by sampling, the meaning of sampling rate and sample resolution, why analogue sound must be converted to binary, and calculating audio file sizes.

blocks.content: Sound is a **wave** — a continuous (analogue) vibration of air. To store it, a computer measures the wave many times per second and stores each measurement as a binary number.

items.title: Sampling
items.content: Measuring the **amplitude** (height) of the sound wave at **regular intervals**.

items.title: Sampling rate
items.content: The **number of samples taken per second**, measured in hertz (Hz). CD quality = 44 100 Hz (44.1 kHz).

items.title: Sample resolution (bit depth)
items.content: The **number of bits used to store each sample**. More bits → more possible amplitude levels (2ⁿ levels). CD quality = 16 bits.

blocks.title: Effect of sampling rate and resolution
rows: Closer to the original wave; high frequencies captured
More accurate amplitude, less "noise", greater dynamic range

theory.title: Why analogue sound must be converted to binary

items: Computers can only store and process **digital (binary) data**; sound in the real world is **analogue** (continuous).
An **ADC** (analogue-to-digital converter), e.g. in a microphone input or sound card, samples the signal and converts each sample to binary.
To play the sound, a **DAC** (digital-to-analogue converter) turns the binary values back into an analogue signal for the speakers.
Digital sound can be **edited, compressed, copied without loss of quality** and transmitted over networks.

8000 × 8 × 10 × 1 = 640 000 bits = 80 000 bytes ≈ **78.1 KiB**
